extracted.intended_audience: students or practitioners of arithmetic/progression problems (historical Italian mathematical readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of procedural rules and worked examples for computing terms, sums, and inverse queries (finding number of terms/days, meeting times, totals) in arithmetic/geometric-style progressions and proportional copying problems, presented in early-modern Italian style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressione continua
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for a continuous progression in which successive terms follow a fixed additive/multiplicative law so that each day (term) certain units are added according to the pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how to compute the number of miles/units after many days by continuing the progression, how to form the sequence of terms and sum them, and how the last term and the number of occurrences depend on the pattern. Examples: two travellers where each day one increases by a fixed amount (binary/ternary/quaternary), and calculating in how many days the accumulated miles reach a given amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regula Duplandi (rule of doubling)
rubrics_metrics.description: A procedure for duplicating (doubling) the successive contributions of antecedent terms so that the frequent term always doubles all preceding ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the units in a table from the first to the last term, then repeatedly double according to the rule; sum and multiply as indicated to obtain totals. Applied to examples of successive doubling of daily contributions or copies (coffee/grains) to compute the value after many duplications. The text gives a concise procedural description under headings like 'Regula Duplandi' and 'Regula Duplandi oomou fiue locafcad?crij breuio'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dupla / Tripla / Quadrupla (multiplicative progression rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for forming progressions where each new term is double/triple/quadruple (or other integer multiple) of a previous term or of the day's unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how to compute the sequence and its sum when the progression multiplies by fixed integers (dupla, tripla, quadrupla), and how to translate those multiplicative steps into total miles/units after a given number of days. Numerous worked numeric examples illustrate applying these multiplicative factors to terms and totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding number of days/terms from a given total or last term (inverse progression problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures to determine how many terms (days) are needed so that the progression's sum or its last term equals a specified quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly poses 'Dimando in quanti giorni...' and demonstrates solving by expressing the sum/last term in terms of the number of terms, using the progression rules (additive or multiplicative), then inverting to find the number of days. Examples include travellers' total miles, paghe (payments) produced by progression rules, and other practical inverse problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular arrangement and grouping to compute progression sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a table of antecedent units (placing units for each term) and group/collapse columns to compute sums efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions show how to put units in a table from the first up to the last term, then collect (recolg) and combine these units by multiplication and addition to find the total. The method is illustrated in many examples where columns representing antecedent terms are multiplied and summed to form the total value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing encounters/meeting times for travelers in progressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for determining when and where two or more travellers (companions) meet, when each advances according to its own progression of daily distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple worked problems consider companions who increase daily by progression rules (e.g., one adds one mile per day, the other two, etc.), including day/night cycles and differing starting positions; the method is to model each traveller's cumulative distance as a term of a progression and solve for the time (day) when their cumulative distances coincide. The text gives specific numeric cases and reductions to manageable computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining companions' progressions (paired/grouped sequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for treating several progressions simultaneously by pairing companions and computing combined effects or totals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how to form combined totals when multiple people each follow their own progression: consider pairing, compute each pair's progression and then aggregate by the given rules (doubling/adding), with examples of how many paghe/payments or miles result from the combined sequence of companions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic/cyclical motion and day-night return modelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for problems with periodic motion where an actor moves forward by day and returns by night (or similar cycles), affecting net progress and encounter counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied notably to the 'topo e gatta' (mouse and cat) example: the mouse climbs during the day and descends at night, the cat moves differently; the text shows how to account for growth of the tree (height) and daily/ nightly movements to compute when encounters occur and cumulative distances relative to the growth process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated copying / exponential growth computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for sequences generated by repeated copying or replication (each copy producing more copies), leading to very large totals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with examples like copying coffee cups/grains many times: place initial counts, then apply repeated duplication/multiplication rules to obtain enormous numbers; the text demonstrates how to track successive multiplications and how to express the final totals (including numeric examples and very large integers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding collected units in a given proportion (recollection in proportion problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques to find how many units are collected when units grow in a specified proportional relationship across terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections titled like 'TRouame vn numero dx recolte le fue vnita in trà p2opo2rionc' show how to set up the first term(s) and apply the given proportional multiplicative pattern to compute the total collected units, using the progression multiplication/addition rules and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction by abatement (abattendo) and modular reduction of terms/days
rubrics_metrics.description: A technique of reducing the problem by subtracting or 'abating' whole days/terms or grouping terms to simplify counting of encounters or totals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple passages recommend 'abatti' (abate) days or parts of sequences and compute the remaining effect to simplify finding when certain events occur or what totals will be, with examples showing group reductions (e.g., looking at differences between days and nights, or collapsing groups of terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of small worked numeric examples to validate procedural rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated recommendation to test the stated rules by working small concrete numeric examples (e.g., small numbers of days, small multiplicative factors) to observe and confirm the progression behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the text the author demonstrates each rule with small-scale examples (specific mile counts, small numbers of days, counts of grains/cups) and shows how the tabular/grouping procedures and multiplications yield the stated totals; the examples serve as both illustration and validation/anti-pattern check against fallacious reasoning.
